evidence: Compared DRAFT.txt with SOURCE.txt word by word. The words it replaces: 'Conscious agreement, unconscious receptivity, emotional compliance, legal and ethical consent. Can people have their minds influenced without conscious agreement of their adult self?' The draft: the same words with '... consent - can people have their minds influenced without the conscious agreement of their adult self?' There are exactly two differences. (1) The full stop and capital 'Can' become a spaced dash and lowercase 'can', which is the change the_change names (the four kinds joined to the question with a dash). (2) 'the' is added before 'conscious agreement'. That one is not named in the_change, but it is meaning-neutral: the 'conscious agreement' it points to is the first item of the list, as it already was, and it adds no claim, condition, person or number. All four terms are there, unchanged and in his order, with 'legal and ethical consent' still one item; 'people', 'their minds', 'influenced', 'without' and 'their adult self' are unchanged. Nothing added, nothing dropped, no change in who does what. Against his published guide: the guide gives four separate sentences ('X is one thing... another') and asserts 'A mind can be influenced without the adult self having clearly chosen the influence', while the passage lists the four and asks the question. That compression and the assertion-to-question move are already in the words it replaces, so this swap neither adds them nor makes them worse, and the_change does not claim to restore them; I note it only so it is not mistaken for something this change did. CONTEXT.txt holds the draft once, verbatim, as the paragraph after the FTC/OECD one. It reads as the natural pivot from the OECD sentence ('steer, deceive, coerce, or manipulate people toward choices that may work against their interests') to the question of agreement, and leads into the Silva quote that answers it by implication. The spaced dash also appears in the paragraph before (the other proposed change) but does a different job there (an appositive), so it is not an unearned repeat. TELL ROWS: went through T01 to T29 and C01 to C04 on the literal draft in context and found none PRESENT. Weighed specifically: T12 and T21 (a four-term list plus a question could look like a closed taxonomy or a packed sentence, but the four are his published four, not extended, not closed with a fifth item and not framed as 'these are the kinds', and the sentence does one job: name the terms and ask); T25 (the dash joins a real list to its question, there is no staged reveal); T24 (a real reader's question, not answered flatly in the next line); T02 and T03 (one distinctions-plus-question unit, set up by the OECD sentence before it, not a run of compressed lessons); T26 ('conscious agreement' recurs inside the sentence, and the added 'the' makes the second a deliberate back-reference to the first item); T07 (the dash is punctuation, not staged filler); the other rows have nothing to match. LINTER FINDINGS: (1) 'B4/E15 list or packed sentence' accepted: the list is the content (his four terms, the same list the words it replaces already hold), cutting any term would lose his meaning, splitting it back into his four sentences would be a different change from the one proposed, and the sentence packs only a list and one question, not several argumentative jobs. (2) 'D9 follows the source order' accepted: it is a punctuation-level rewrite of the words it replaces, so it follows them by construction, and the thing that is noticed is the question itself. Residual note only: the change is very small, so whether it moves the detector reading is a detector question, not a preservation one. PASS.
